references.text: Jesus is referred to as "Lord" (ὁ κύριος), a title that Luke uses repeatedly for Jesus, emphasizing his divine authority.
Jesus was deeply moved with compassion (ἐσπλαγχνίσθη) toward the crowds, using the same expression as when he showed compassion to the widow at Nain.
Jesus had deep compassion for the sick and healed them—the same profound mercy he shows toward the widow.
Jesus says he has deep compassion (σπλαγχνίζομαι) for the crowd that has no food—demonstrating Jesus' repeated mercy.
Jesus was deeply moved with compassion for the leper and healed him—the same profound mercy that drives Jesus to act.
Jesus says "Do not weep" (Μὴ κλαίετε) to those mourning Jairus' daughter, the same exhortation he gives to the widow at Nain.
Jesus was deeply moved and wept at Lazarus' tomb—showing the same deep compassion for grieving people.
God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or sorrow—the ultimate fulfillment of Jesus' care for those who mourn.
The Lord comforts Rachel as she weeps over her children and tells her to stop weeping—a parallel to Jesus' exhortation "Do not weep" directed at a grieving mother.
The Lord will swallow up death forever and wipe away tears from all faces—the background for Jesus' power over death and his comfort to the mourning.
Elijah raises the widow of Zarephath's dead son back to life—a close parallel to Jesus raising the widow's son at Nain, which Luke clearly alludes to.
Elisha raises the Shunammite woman's son from the dead—another Old Testament parallel where a prophet shows compassion to a mother and raises her son.
